items.title: Clashes Erupt Again in France, After Festive Start to Day of Protest
items.summary: More than 300,000 people took to the streets, some wearing Halloween costumes, before the demonstrations ended in violence.
items.full_text:
Title: Clashes Erupt Again in France, After Festive Start to Day of Protest - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/world/europe/france-protests-clashes.html

Published Time: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 22:25:31 GMT

Markdown Content:
Hundreds of thousands of people poured into the streets of French cities again on Saturday for protests that began with the festivity of a Halloween parade but gave way to darker scenes of clashes between demonstrators and the police.

The violence fell well short of the arson and looting that engulfed Paris and other cities on Oct. 17, when a mass demonstration muted into widespread lawlessness. The crowds, estimated by the government at 320,000, were also smaller than on the previous two Saturdays of nationwide protest.

Still, the turnout — and the chaos — was significant enough to suggest that France remains in the grip of acute unrest, nearly two months into a protest movement that began with rebellious high school students.

In several cities, the police fired tear gas and sprayed water cannons to disperse some protesters after what had been peaceful rallies. In Paris, 200 to 300 rioters, masked and clad in black, skirmished with police officers into the evening, lobbing Molotov cocktails, fireworks and other projectiles.

It was a discordant end to a day that had begun on an upbeat, even joyful, note. Many people made the most of the fact that the demonstration coincided with Halloween. They showed up in eye-catching costumes, as Spider-Man, Zorro or the Pink Panther, dancing as often as they marched. One, dressed as Marie Antoinette, held a sign that said, “Let them eat cake.”

French officials had said they worried that the holiday would introduce a dangerous element, since demonstrators might conceal their faces. They marshaled 70,000 police officers, the same number as last week, and shifted routes to keep the protesters away from city centers.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, condemned what he said were violent rioters, with links to the far left, who mixed in with the protesters. Many of them broke into clashes with the police as the marches ended and the authorities tried to disperse the crowds.

Image

Taking cover behind a sign in Paris as fireworks exploded on Saturday.Credit...Sameer Al-Doumy/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

On Saturday evening, Mr. Nuñez said, the police in Paris were still confronting “groups that intend to head to the Bastille,” the site of an uprising in 1789 that is a milestone in the French Revolution. The Paris authorities had prevented the march from starting there.

“The intent is to create an insurrectionary climate — a quasi-revolutionary atmosphere — and to attack domestic security forces in order to gain access to stores, to carry out looting, to attack public buildings, and they are attacking law enforcement in an extremely violent manner,” Mr. Nuñez said.

In Paris, television images showed the police coming under attack by fireworks and Molotov cocktails. At least one officer was briefly engulfed in flames, an attack that Mr. Nuñez said qualified as attempted murder. Trash bins were set alight, as was a car. Similar chaotic scenes played out in Marseille, Rennes, Nantes, Toulouse, Montpellier, Angers and Tours.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader and presidential candidate, condemned the targeting of police officers, writing on social media that the “perpetrators of this attack must be found and sentenced with the utmost severity.”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a far-left leader who is also running for president, accused the government of undercounting the crowds. He claimed they were as large as previous demonstrations, despite the change in the route.

The police arrested 565 people, which Mr. Nuñez said prevented a worse outbreak of violence. The authorities also carried out 40,000 spot checks across the country to prevent people from taking weapons to protest areas.

But Mr. Nuñez was careful not to declare victory. The Interior Ministry warned that the violence could intensify long after darkness fell. On Saturday night, bands of people still roamed Paris and other cities. “We will remain vigilant throughout the evening and the night,” he said.

Image

Demonstrators and officers faced off in Paris on Saturday. Officials marshaled 70,000 police officers to try to keep order.Credit...Pierre Crom/Getty Images

It was a stark contrast to earlier in the day, when people began massing for the marches. Brass bands played music, and the protesters’ costumes provided a celebratory atmosphere. Several people said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17, when the marches mutated into violence, with gangs smashing shop windows and looting the contents.

“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who had dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”

Arthur Fleury, a 20-year-old literature student, came as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wearing a mask of Ms. Le Pen, the far-right leader. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

As the crowd marched along its route in eastern Paris, a bystander dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers. But there were already signs of trouble. Half a dozen masked protesters in black pushed trash bins, one of which was burning, into the middle of the crowd. They set a second bin on fire near where a police unit was stationed.

Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, precipitating a small clash with the masked group. “That’s no way to protest,” said one of those who helped put out the fire.

Among the protesters were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom wore white outfits identifying them as “street medics” able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she participating because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school.

Image

Demonstrations in Paris on Saturday began with a celebratory air, but officials were worried from the start about the confluence of Halloween and the protests.Credit...Ed Jones/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he joined after his younger brother told him he was tear-gassed and almost struck by a stun grenade at a protest this month.

“The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So, I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.”

On Saturday, the two said they saw one person who had been injured in the head. Help arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said.

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

items.title: North Korean Hackers Stole Billions, the F.B.I. Says. It’s Not Their First Heist.
items.summary: This week’s $6.3 billion hack of Binance is the largest to hit crypto, and would be the most that North Koreans have stolen in years of brazen cybercrime.
items.full_text:
Title: North Korean Hackers Stole Billions, the F.B.I. Says. It’s Not Their First Heist. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/world/asia/north-korea-hacking.html

Published Time: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 22:26:03 GMT

Markdown Content:
Poor, isolated and heavily sanctioned, North Korea is not a country you would expect to field an elite army of hackers capable of pulling off billion-dollar heists.

But for years, security officials had warned that the regime’s cyberattacks were becoming increasingly sophisticated, looting enormous sums to support North Korea’s military and nuclear weapons program.

Those fears peaked this week when Binance, the world’s [largest cryptocurrency exchange](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/technology/binance-hack-crypto.html), announced that hackers had made off with some $6 billion in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. The F.B.I. [said on Saturday](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2026/north-korea-responsible-for-6-billion-binance-attack) that North Korea was responsible for the attack in the first official acknowledgment of the regime’s role.

Powered by a pipeline of top-class programming students, North Korea’s hacking units have penetrated banks and companies and capitalized on the rise of crypto. A U.N. panel in 2024 found the [regime’s cyberattacks](https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n24/032/68/pdf/n2403268.pdf) had generated about half its foreign currency income, amounting to billions in revenue. Experts agree that the regime is now one of the biggest and most capable [cyber threats](https://www.38north.org/2026/01/from-digital-kleptocracy-to-rogue-crypto-superpower/) in the world.

As investigators dig into the Binance attack, here is a look at some of the most famous North Korean hacks.

## 2014: The Sony Attack

Image

The computers of Sony Pictures, which was behind the film “The Interview,” about the assassination of North Korea’s leader, were hacked in 2014.Credit...Damian Dovarganes/Associated Press

In 2014, the tech and media giant Sony Pictures was preparing to release “The Interview,” a far-fetched comedy about the assassination of the North’s leader.

Then, American officials said, hackers associated with the Lazarus Group, a shadowy hacking syndicate backed by the North Korean government, breached the [company’s computers](https://www.sipa.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/2022-11/Sony%20-%20Written%20Case.pdf).

The attacks caused the leaks of internal documents containing salary information that humiliated top company officials and stole terabytes of data.

North Korea has never formally taken responsibility for the attack. At the time, however, Kim Jong-un, the country’s dictator, called the film an “act of terrorism.”

## 2016: Custom Malware

In 2016, North Korean hackers tried to steal about $1 billion from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Only a spelling error stopped them.

Using a payment messaging system known as SWIFT, the hackers were able to persuade the New York Fed to move money to accounts in the Philippines. The hackers were looting an account of the Bangladesh Central Bank when bankers grew suspicious about a withdrawal request that had misspelled “foundation” as “fandation.”

Still, the hackers made off with $81 million from the central bank of Bangladesh.

The attack was important because it showed how savvy North Korean hackers were becoming. In contrast to off-the-shelf tools that had been used in other attacks at the time, the malware the thieves devised for this heist was a custom code, configured for a specific bank. Written from scratch, it was unfamiliar to existing [virus-protection programs](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/05/03/magazine/money-issue-bangladesh-billion-dollar-bank-heist.html).

## Crypto Booms and Busts

As the cryptocurrency market boomed in the mid 2010s, North Korea began targeting firms in the industry, escalating to large-scale attacks on crypto exchanges by 2020, according to a North Korea-focused publication of the Stimson Center, a Washington-based think tank.

North Korean hackers were accused of stealing [$571 million](https://undocs.org/Home/Mobile?FinalSymbol=S%2F2019%2F171&Language=E&DeviceType=Desktop&LangRequested=False) from crypto exchanges between January 2017 and September 2018 and [$316 million](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/s_2021_211.pdf) from 2019 to November 2020.

Image

Gamers playing Axie Infinity, a blockchain-based, play-to-earn video game in which players win tokens that can be exchanged for cryptocurrency.Credit...Jam Sta Rosa/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

With borders shut because of the coronavirus pandemic and traditional banks strengthening their firewalls against hackers, cryptocurrency theft was becoming an increasingly vital source of foreign currency for the regime.

In 2022, the United States [publicly accused](https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/press-releases/fbi-statement-on-attribution-of-malicious-cyber-activity-posed-by-the-democratic-peoples-republic-of-korea) the Lazarus Group of stealing $620 million in cryptocurrency from the video game Axie Infinity.

That year, North Korea’s haul was a little under [$1 billion](https://blog.chainalysis.com/reports/chainalysis-web3-report-preview-safety-compliance-defi/?utm_campaign=twitter&utm_source=OrganicSocial&utm_content=Thread), according to Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, which found 50 percent of the industry’s yearly losses were from North Korean hacks.

Given the history of spectacular market crashes, crypto is hardly a stable source of funding. But at a time when North Korea had locked itself down during the pandemic, hacking crypto exchanges allowed it to generate income in ways that were both Covid-safe and harder to trace in an industry subject to limited government oversight.

## 2025: The Bybit Attack

In February 2025, North Korean hackers pulled off what was then the biggest heist in the crypto industry’s history, stealing $1.5 billion in cryptocurrencies, according to the F.B.I.

To [pull off the breach](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/06/technology/bybit-crypto-hack-north-korea.html), the hackers exploited the cryptocurrency exchange ByBit’s reliance on a free software product.

The [North Korean hackers had tricked](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/06/technology/bybit-crypto-hack-north-korea.html) the chief executive of Bybit, Ben Zhou, into authorizing a seemingly routine transaction that handed them control of the exchange’s system.

Image

Ben Zhou, Bybit’s chief executive, at a conference in 2024.Credit...Tamir Kalifa for The New York Times

After looting Bybit, the North Korean hackers spread the stolen funds across a vast web of online crypto wallets, a money-laundering strategy that they had also employed after other heists.

## 2026: The Binance Hack

This week, that record was broken in the Binance hack. The F.B.I. on Saturday accused the North Korean hacking unit, TraderTraitor, which [the bureau](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-108a) has said is another name for the Lazarus Group, of carrying out the attack.

Hackers stole $6.3 billion in an attack that used “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” Chainalysis wrote in a blog [post](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/binance-exploit-latest-findings-and-response/) on Friday.

In a statement, the F.B.I. said it had observed “TraderTraitor” actors converting stolen assets into Ethereum. The bureau added that it expects those assets will be “further laundered.”

The [specifics of the attack](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/business/binance-hack-crypto-price-what.html) are still being established. Binance initially [said](https://x.com/binance/status/2115993361517891592) that the hackers might have compromised an engineer’s laptop, leading to unauthorized withdrawals. But in an update [on social media](https://x.com/binance/status/2116089661408108712) on Friday, the company said it had identified “additional points of breach.”
